query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys, simultaneous resistance to wear and corrosion in harsh environments is governed by the formation of a dynamically-induced ultra‐nanocrystalline surface layer that both reduces shear-related mechanical degradation and facilitates rapid passivation against corrosive attack.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase coarse-grained CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to controlled sliding wear in a corrosive (chloride-containing) environment versus an inert environment.
generation.conditions: Identical mechanical loading and sliding conditions are used; one set of samples is tested in an inert atmosphere while another set is immersed in a corrosive solution, ensuring that differences in degradation arise from the coupling of wear and corrosion effects.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an ultra‐nanocrystalline near-surface layer as induced by dynamic amorphization during wear.
generation.mechanism: Under mechanical sliding, the coarse-grained alloy undergoes dynamic amorphization that refines the surface grains. This ultra‐nanocrystalline layer lowers the shear strength (yielding lower friction and wear) and promotes the formation of a stable, self-healing, passive oxide film that retards corrosive attack. Thus, the layer acts as a mediator that couples improved mechanical resistance with enhanced corrosion passivation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under corrosive mechanical loading, the alloy should exhibit lower wear volumes and reduced corrosion current densities compared to a baseline inert environment (or compared to materials that do not form such a layer). The synergy between mechanical wear and corrosion will be less severe than expected based on the sum of individual wear or corrosion phenomena because the protective nano-layer continuously renews and passivates newly exposed surfaces.
generation.baseline: The same alloy subjected to identical sliding wear tests in an inert (non-corrosive) environment.
generation.boundary: This behavior is predicted to hold under moderate loads and sliding speeds that support dynamic layer formation; it may fail under extreme mechanical loads or temperatures that either prevent the formation or cause rapid breakdown of the ultra‐nanocrystalline layer, or in alloys with pre-existing microstructural defects that inhibit dynamic amorphization.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence supports low wear under inert conditions via dynamic amorphization, the precise quantitative impact of the layer on corrosion passivation under combined degradation is less well defined and may vary with the corrosive medium and stress conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple CoCrFeMnNi HEA samples with identical dimensions and microstructures. Subject one group to sliding wear tests under inert atmosphere and another in a controlled chloride-rich aqueous environment, keeping load, sliding speed, and test duration constant. Use STEM to analyze the near-surface microstructure post-test.
measurements: Corrosion current density via potentiodynamic polarization
Grain size and phase composition of the near-surface layer using STEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, under corrosive conditions, the alloy fails to form an ultra‐nanocrystalline layer or if the wear and corrosion metrics show significantly higher degradation (i.e. substantially higher wear volume and corrosion current density) compared to the inert baseline, then the hypothesized protective mechanism is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
